In the canteen of their Hyderabad school, Irawati announced it with total confidence: "The board is cancelling practical exams this year. It's confirmed."
Asif stopped eating. "Who confirmed it?"
Irawati opened her mouth, and nothing came. She had heard it so many times that it felt as solid as the times table. Was it a teacher? A cousin?
That night she scrolled back through the family group. There it was, forwarded four times by different relatives, in red capitals: "BREAKING! SHARE WITH ALL STUDENTS." No name, no notice number.
The next morning the class teacher pinned up the real circular: practicals as usual, in March.
Irawati found Asif at the gate. "I only believed it because I kept seeing it. I didn't even remember where it came from."

qa.q: What did the class teacher's circular say?
qa.a: Practicals as usual, in March.

qa.q: Why did Irawati feel so sure the practicals were cancelled?
qa.a: She had seen the claim so many times that it felt as solid as the times table, even though she could not remember where it came from.

qa.q: What was Irawati's turning point, and what could she do next time?
qa.a: Being unable to answer Asif's "Who confirmed it?"; next time she could ask herself that before repeating a claim and look for an official notice.

qa.q: How might Asif have been affected if he had believed Irawati?
qa.a: Asif might have stopped preparing for the practicals and been caught out in March because of a forward.

grounding: It shows a teenager repeating a claim as fact because it feels familiar, having forgotten it came from a forwarded message.

"Ma, don't cook that rice," Rafiq said from the kitchen door. "They're making fake rice out of plastic now. You can bounce it like a ball."
His mother, Vinita, kept stirring. "Who told you?"
"Everyone knows it."
"Everyone who?"
Rafiq thought. "I've heard it loads of times."
"Heard it, or read it?"
He pulled out his phone and scrolled. "Here. The colony group. And here, the cricket group. And here, from Nanu." Three forwards of the same video.
"So one video, three times," Vinita said. "Did anyone test it? Or say where it came from?"
Rafiq read them again. "No." He rubbed his neck. "It just felt true because I kept seeing it."
"Then let's roll a ball of this rice after dinner and see if it bounces."

qa.a: In the colony group, the cricket group and a forward from Nanu, the same video three times.

qa.a: He had seen the claim so often that it felt like common knowledge, and he had forgotten it all came from one forwarded video.

Francis, you're writing your first big essay, so let old Samir uncle tell you something from my college days.
I was twenty and wrote a paper on village markets. There was one line I was very proud of: "A market is a newspaper you can eat." My professor circled it and wrote, "Beautiful. Whose is it?" I was offended. It was mine, I thought.
Months later I reopened a book of essays my roommate had given me. There it was on page thirty, word for word. I had read it once, liked it and forgotten I'd ever read it. My mind kept the line and threw away the label.
I went to the professor and told him. He said, "Good. Now you know why we keep a source notebook." I've kept one ever since. Start yours today.

qa.q: What did the professor write beside Samir's line?
qa.a: The professor wrote, "Beautiful. Whose is it?"

qa.q: Why was Samir offended at first by the professor's question?
qa.a: He had read the line once, liked it and forgotten reading it, so it honestly felt like his own creation.

qa.a: The professor seemed pleased, treating it as an honest slip worth learning from and using it to explain the source notebook.

Thursday, 10 pm
Long day at the transport office. Jatin was sure the new bus route cut travel time by half. "Everyone's saying it," he said. I asked, "How do we know?" He rolled his eyes and called me "Madam Footnote" again.
But I tried my own trick on myself tonight. For the report I made three columns: what I saw (I rode the route twice, 42 and 47 minutes), what I was told (drivers say "much faster"), and what I'm guessing (maybe fewer stops?). The old route data says 55 minutes. So: faster, yes. Half? No.
A year ago I'd have written "half" too, because it sounded right. I'll show Jatin the draft tomorrow and let the columns do the arguing.
Amandeep

qa.a: Amandeep rode the route twice, and it took 42 and 47 minutes.

qa.a: Three columns: what she saw, what she was told and what she's guessing, then a check against the old route data.

Six months after their metro train stalled in a tunnel for forty minutes, Ojas and Trisha sat in a Delhi café and found they couldn't agree on anything.
"The lights went out completely," Ojas said. "Pitch dark."
"No, the emergency lights were on," Trisha said. "And a baby was crying the whole time."
"There was no baby. It was an old man coughing."
Each was completely sure. Each had been scared that day.
Trisha pulled up the short video she had filmed inside the coach. Dim white lights. A child singing softly. No crying baby, no coughing man.
They stared, then laughed. "We were both so certain," Ojas said. "I guess being frightened makes you sure, not right."

qa.q: What did Trisha's video show?
qa.a: Dim white lights and a child singing softly, with no crying baby and no coughing man.

qa.q: Why was each friend so certain of their own version?
qa.a: Both had been scared in the tunnel, and that fear made their memories feel sharp and sure, even where they were wrong.

qa.q: What did the video teach them, and how could they use it next time?
qa.a: That being frightened makes you sure, not right; next time they could look for a record before insisting.

qa.q: What might Ojas feel seeing a dimly lit coach in the video after insisting it was pitch dark?
qa.a: Ojas might feel surprised and a little embarrassed, but relieved to laugh about it with Trisha instead of arguing.

Dear Harish,

So I did what I should have done before shouting: I asked Anita Aunty for her video. It's you, Harish. You gave the speech. I'm holding the garland and crying in the background.
I'm sorry I called you a show-off. That day matters so much to me that I think my memory put me at the centre. It's still one of my best memories, and I'm keeping it. I'm just not using it to win arguments any more.
Love, your sister Parul

passage:
On Sunday night, in their Mumbai flat, Vaibhav sat on the bed and repeated the Hindi poem forty times for Monday's recitation. By ten o'clock the words came out smoothly. "Done!" Vaibhav told Indu didi.
On Monday the recitation went well.
On Friday the teacher said, "Surprise! Say it again for parents' day." Vaibhav stood up, said the first line and froze. The rest had gone, like chalk wiped off a board.
At home Indu didi smiled. "When I learn poems, I say them for ten minutes a day, for five days. It feels slow, but they stay."
Vaibhav frowned, then took the book out again. "Ten minutes. Starting today."

qa.q: How many times did Vaibhav repeat the poem on Sunday night?
qa.a: Vaibhav repeated it forty times.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav feel "Done!" on Sunday night?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt confident and relieved because the words were coming out smoothly by ten o'clock, so the poem felt learned, even though it had all been packed into one evening.

qa.q: What does Indu didi suggest, and why does it work better?
qa.a: Ten minutes a day for five days; spreading it out makes the poem stay, even if it feels slower.

qa.q: What might the teacher think on seeing Vaibhav freeze on Friday?
qa.a: The teacher may be surprised, since Monday went well, and may guess the poem was crammed rather than truly learned.

grounding: It shows a child who learns a poem in one evening, recites it the next day and loses it within days.
